content: #43234 shows that, in characteristic 0, the bundle of continuous alternating maps between C^n vector bundles is C^n. I was surprised that I needed characteristic 0: we have already the bundle as a continuous bundle, and no characteristic assumption is needed there. Fortunately, Bourbaki makes the same assumption (although he never says where it's needed, because it's a book of results without proofs), so it's probably reasonable.

Of course, it's too big for a single PR, so I've split a few prerequisites in #43338, about smoothness results for different maps related to alternating maps, in vector spaces (+300, -9). I can split it further if it helps.

It's an interesting exercise to see what breaks up in positive characteristic. To say that the bundle is analytic means that the coordinate changes should be analytic. It boils down to the following: consider the precomposition by a linear map, on spaces of alternating maps (in Lean terms, (E →L[𝕜] F) → (F [⋀^ι]→L[𝕜] G) →L[𝕜] (E [⋀^ι]→L[𝕜] G), mapping f to the map mapping m (v_1, ..., v_i) to m (f v_1, ...., f v_i)). Is this map analytic as a function of f? I can not prove it in positive characteristic when the spaces are not finite-dimensional.

With AI assistance (and some insight from @Yaël Dillies), I was able to prove the necessary lemma without the [CharZero] assumption in all but the CωC^\omegaCω case: #43548

theorem contDiff_compContinuousLinearMapCLM {n : ℕ∞} :
    ContDiff 𝕜 n (compContinuousLinearMapCLM :
      (E →L[𝕜] E') → (E' [⋀^ι]→L[𝕜] F) →L[𝕜] (E [⋀^ι]→L[𝕜] F))

However one step of the proof relies on induction on the smoothness n, which is why the proof does not extend to the analytic case. Specifically, the following lemma is by induction:

theorem comp_contDiff_iff.{uE, uF, uG} {E : Type uE} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
    {F : Type uF} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F]
    {G : Type uG} [NormedAddCommGroup G] [NormedSpace 𝕜 G]
    (Φ : E →ₗᵢ[𝕜] F) (hΦ : IsClosed (range Φ)) {n : ℕ∞} {f : G → E} :
    ContDiff 𝕜 n (Φ ∘ f) ↔ ContDiff 𝕜 n f

I think it is not very surprising that the result holds in the n≠ωn\neq\omegan=ω case, precisely because of this lemma (which I noticed we were lacking while reviewing Sebastien’s PR, and which should be generalized to a linear docs#IsClosedEmbedding), which is not clearly true in postitive-characteristic for analytic functions. The interesting question is really here.

Also it is a bit surprising to me that you would prove this by induction: I think with the right API this should follow directly from the definition of docs#HasFTaylorSeriesUpTo.

Note that I am not writing these comments for you to feed them to an LLM; so please don’t.
Note that in positive characteristic the only interesting case is analytic, because otherwise manifolds are badly behaved.

Update:
After several months of LLM-assisted search (I have been working on this problem on-and-off since July), I have found a counter-example to the ContinuousAlternatingMap.contDiff_compContinuousLinearMapCLM theorem.

Summary of Counter-Example

On the other hand, since every element in FFF has finite rank, we can approximate by a rank r<∞r<\inftyr<∞ matrix ||Φ(a,b,a,b)−R∣∣<1\Phi(a,b,a,b) - R|| < 1Φ(a,b,a,b)−R∣∣<1, which leads to a contradiction for t>rt > rt>r.

An 10-page write-up relying only on elementary math is available here (drafted by Claude, heavily revised by me). A formalization can be found here.

In fact, I have a stronger result than this, but I am waiting to release the paper since I have not yet had the time to properly rewrite the mathslop. However, I have lean certificates of the following theorems for all characteristic-p, nontrivially normed fields kkk:

  1. The bifunctor Altι:Veckop×Veck→Veck\text{Alt}^\iota : \text{Vec}_k^{op} \times \text{Vec}_k \to \text{Vec}_kAltι:Veckop​×Veck​→Veck​ is CωC^\omegaCω if and only if p>∣ι∣p > |\iota|p>∣ι∣.
  1. The contravariant functor Altι(−;k):Veckop→Veck\text{Alt}^\iota (-;k) : \text{Vec}_k^{op} \to \text{Vec}_kAltι(−;k):Veckop​→Veck​ is CωC^\omegaCω if and only if p>∣ι∣p > |\iota|p>∣ι∣ or kkk is spherically complete.
  1. The bifunctor Altι:Veckop×Veck∘→Veck\text{Alt}^\iota : \text{Vec}_k^{op} \times \text{Vec}_k^\circ \to \text{Vec}_kAltι:Veckop​×Veck∘​→Veck​ is always CωC^\omegaCω, where Veck∘\text{Vec}_k^\circVeck∘​ denotes the category of spherically complete, ultranormed kkk vector spaces.

The above results also hold if we work in the category of Banach spaces instead of arbitrary vector spaces.

I will be giving a talk for lean.nyc at NYU this Sunday where I will elaborate more fully on the proofs, how they were found, and what it means for alternating bundles / differential forms in Mathlib. I will also pose some related conjectures about continuous alternating map bundles. The event will be recorded for those interested in watching.

For context, do I understand correctly that contDiff_compContinuousLinearMapCLM is a conjecture which is only written down in this zulip topic (i.e. not as proof_wantedin mathlib or in formal-conjectures) and the PRs #43338 and #43234 by Sébastien Gouëzel linked above and in your paper prove a special case thereof. I was a bit confused by a "counterexample to a theorem" at first

Call it a "folklore conjecture" if you will. The first place it was mentioned on this Zulip was February, 2025 #maths > Last step; Smoothness of vector bundle of alternating maps. It then later appeared in @Yury G. Kudryashov's DeRham Cohomology repo.

As Sébastien mention's above, the finite-dimensional / characteristic 0 assumption dates back to Bourbaki, so this could also be seen as attempt to generalize their work.

The conjecture was rather that it was not analytic, so you are confirming the conjecture, not giving a counterexample. This is great. You should definitely cite Bourbaki, where they explicitly say they don't know the answer, because answering a question in Bourbaki does not happen every day!
Is my own conjecture, namely that it becomes analytic once you fix the definition of derivative as we talked about in London, correct?

@Yaël Dillies I still haven't found a satisfactory definition of derivative that makes this statement true. As Anatole discusses above, C∞C^\inftyC∞ smoothness does pull back along a closed embedding (cf. the diagram below). However, I don't think we can make CωC^\omegaCω satisfy this same property.
